title: Sikh Dharma in the West
hook: Western converts since the 1970s, often in white turbans

segments.voice: Yesterday, two movements with one name, and your line was know the difference. Did you catch a mix-up and set it straight? Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.

A gurdwara in New Mexico, or California, or Massachusetts. A woman in a white turban leads the kirtan, and her Gurmukhi is careful and clear. Her parents were not Sikhs. Neither were the parents of the man beside her on the tabla, who took a Sikh name as an adult. After the program, they serve langar alongside Punjabi families whose grandparents came from villages near Amritsar. Everyone sits in the same rows. Someone visiting for the first time might wonder how this came to be. It's the story of a stream that flows far from Punjab.
screen: `A WHITE TURBAN LEADS THE KIRTAN.` → `PARENTS WHO WERE NOT SIKHS.` → `THE SAME ROWS AT LANGAR.`

segments.voice: Sikh Dharma is the name used by a community of Sikhs in the West, among them people who came to the faith as adults. They first met it through a teacher of yoga and meditation from Punjab, known as Yogi Bhajan. His students took up the rehat: uncut hair, the turban, the daily banis, often an early morning practice before dawn. Women in this community commonly wear the turban too, and white clothing is a familiar sight. Two things need saying plainly. First, Sikhs have held differing views about this community: about the yoga it taught alongside Sikh practice, and about how its customs sit beside the Rehat Maryada. Second, its founder's legacy is now seriously contested. Former students have come forward with grave accusations against him, and the community itself has had to face them. Members have responded in different ways. That is part of the story, and this path won't smooth it over. And yet the newcomers themselves stand on something older than any teacher. Guru Arjan, in Raag Dhanasari on Ang 671, sings, in paraphrase: I have made everyone my friend, and I am a friend to everyone. A gurdwara with open doors and one row at langar was built for exactly this. A stranger walks in, covers their head, sits down, and is fed. Now look back at this week. The Taksal and its careful reading. Santhiaa, sound it right. The Jatha's kirtan till dawn. Nanaksar's continuous praise. The Namdharis, different, and respected. Baba Dayal's reform, and the need to know the difference. And today, newcomers who learned the Guru's word as a second language.
screen: `SIKH DHARMA: WESTERN SIKHS.` · `THE REHAT TAKEN UP AS ADULTS.` · `A CONTESTED FOUNDER.` · `ANG 671: A FRIEND TO EVERYONE.` · then, large: `NEWCOMERS WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome a newcomer. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone new in a place you know well: a new coworker, a new neighbor, someone who just joined a group, class or congregation. Remember what it was like to be the new one, unsure where to sit. Breathe in, and picture yourself showing them one small thing they'd need to know. Breathe out, and picture them sitting down, at ease. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Sikh Dharma in the West. A community of Sikhs in the West, among them people who took up the rehat as adults, often recognized by white dress and turbans worn by women and men. Today's word.
